source.verification_method: All fourteen supplied text pages, all footnotes and 73 references read. The file has no substantive figures/tables. Public arXiv-v1 download matches the supplied 153805-byte SHA exactly. Crossref and institutional/arXiv metadata verify the related proceedings identity. Targeted publisher/catalog/book metadata and a cited-paper first-page byline clarify bibliography errors; no full book or cited empirical study independently read.

citation.title: Who is responsible? Social Identity, Robot Errors and Blame Attribution

reading.source_scope_note: Philosophical analysis of blame, social power, gendered expectations and robot-error repair, drawing on cited HRI literature. No new experiment, systematic-search protocol, participant dataset, quantified carryover effect or tested mitigation is reported.
access_limits: The complete fourteen-page manuscript, footnotes and 73 bibliography entries read. PDF inspection finds no substantive images or tables, only text and footnote rules; no missing statistical figure is inferred.

The public arXiv v1 file is byte-identical to the supplied file. The related final proceedings chapter’s identity, date and locator are metadata checks, not a separate full read or independent replication.

Cited empirical studies are summarized by the authors, often with mixed outcomes, and were not independently fully read here. The Crowell et al. cited-paper author byline on its first page was checked; that is not a complete seven-page study review.

Schank/Abelson book metadata, the University of Pennsylvania Huckleberry Finn catalog and MIT Press author metadata were checked. The full books by Strawson, Rhee, D’Ignazio/Klein, Strengers/Kennedy and others were not read or transcribed.

No original interview/experiment data, code, preregistration or supplement was obtained because the supplied work reports an argument rather than a new data collection. No author contact, source software execution or external message sent.

study.type: Normative/conceptual argument with illustrative cases and a selected literature discussion, not a new participant study, systematic review or meta-analysis. No sample size, effect prevalence or general causal effect is estimated.
study.thesis: Robot identities and repair behavior may transmit descriptive and prescriptive expectations from social hierarchies into HRI and later human interactions. The authors propose that blame practices must attend to power and discrimination rather than merely maximize smooth or efficient interaction.
study.stance: The paper explicitly distinguishes social norms from justified moral norms and also acknowledges that social norms can support cooperation, empathy and protection. It does not show every convention is oppressive or every emotional reaction unjustified.
study.responsibility: A footnote intentionally treats moral responsibility and blame together for this argument. That local simplification does not erase distinctions between causal contribution, blame, answerability, attributability, accountability or repair in the ontology.
study.reactive_attitudes: The Strawsonian framework locates responsibility in interpersonal moral sentiments/demands. The authors criticize idealized equal-standing assumptions and ask whose claims to respect/repair are heard. They also explicitly concede that Strawson’s original paper does not state that social and moral norms are identical.
study.gender: The analysis treats gender as socially structured and focuses mostly on a female/male division because of common design practice, while explicitly acknowledging a wider spectrum of identities. It does not validate gender inference from a voice or claim inherent traits of women, men or nonbinary people.
study.empirical_mixture: Cited work includes some gender/stereotype-congruity effects, nulls and benefits of stereotype mismatch in educational contexts. Agency–blame findings also vary. Preserve this mixed literature rather than conclude all people inevitably prefer compliant female robots or all gendered designs have one effect.
study.carryover: The cited Erel study motivates possible HRI→HHI carryover, but this paper supplies no new carryover design, sample, delay, independent replication or gender-specific blame-transfer estimate. Broader long-term societal claims remain hypotheses/risks.
study.work: Accommodation work denotes practical adaptations by passersby/workers that keep public robot activity possible. It can overlap invisible/care/emotional labor but need not be emotional, unpaid, gendered or exploitative by definition. The quoted delivery-robot field study was not independently read.
study.hypothetical_example: The woman-expected-to-help versus man-praised-for-helping robot vignette illustrates a possible unequal normative expectation. It is not a tested result or proof that an observed individual deserves blame or has a hidden discriminatory motive.
study.scapegoating: The source quotes a definition emphasizing knowingly misplaced blame. That intent component belongs to the cited account; do not silently impose it on every structural responsibility problem or infer knowing blame displacement from an apology, interface preference or aggregate rating.
study.design_proposals: Embracing the glitch, counter-stereotypical robot responses, careful coboting and sociomorphing are proposed interventions/research directions. The paper does not test their efficacy, comparative safety or long-term benefits. Purposefully causing failures or retaliating against users is not authorized by this discussion.
study.intelligent_disobedience: The text names a cited robot-teleoperation framework for acting correctly under faulty/problematic orders. It is a bounded instruction-assessment concept, not permission for an agent to protect its own goals, ignore justified corrections or override authorized stopping instructions.
study.sociomorphing: The conclusion proposes sociality with clearly nonhuman entities, linked to a cited typology. This overlaps the existing Sociomorphism entry; a different noun/verb form does not establish a new mechanism.

summary: Add Reactive attitudes, Social scripts, Accommodation work and Intelligent disobedience with explicit conceptual scope. Keep Sociomorphing connected to Sociomorphism and enrich existing blame/labor records. Preserve mixed cited findings, hypothetical-versus-measured distinctions and the separation of moral justification from role stereotypes.

findings.definition: Interpersonal emotional attitudes that respond to how others regard or treat people.
findings.novelty_rationale: A framework for interpersonal emotional responses differs from assigning blame, a single emotion, forgiveness or general mind attribution. The source explicitly names reactive attitudes and their relation to moral sentiments and interpersonal demands.

evidence.quote: reactive attitudes) play a major role
introducing what he named as the “reactive attitudes.”

findings.evidence_scope: Conceptual reconstruction/critique of responsibility theory, not a new psychological experiment or a validation of emotional responses toward robots. Original Strawson and other cited books were not independently fully read.
findings.boundary: An emotional attitude is not automatically morally justified, accurate or a demand others must satisfy. Role expectations, social hierarchy, legitimate accountability and actual wrong need separate assessment. A generated apology or moral complaint does not establish that AI feels resentment, gratitude or entitlement.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human philosophical/psychological framework; no subjective robot moral emotion or new empirical effect demonstrated
findings.ai_proposal: When an AI interprets blame, gratitude or resentment in a conversation, distinguish the expressed attitude from the evidence for the underlying norm and harm. Explain accountable actions without treating emotional pressure or stereotypes as authority.

findings.definition: Learned representations of familiar social situations that specify expected sequences of actions and roles.
findings.origin: Cognitive psychology / script theory / social interaction
findings.novelty_rationale: A structured expected sequence differs from a single social norm, a stereotype, hidden curriculum or merely taking another’s perspective. The source explicitly defines scripts as familiar predefined sequences shaping expected behavior.

evidence.quote: Scripts can be described as predefined sequences
from familiar scenarios, which influence how actors are imagined to behave

findings.evidence_scope: Background framework applied to HRI and expectations about service/care roles. No dedicated script-learning experiment or unconscious-processing measure is provided. Original Schank/Abelson book identity was checked, not its full text.
findings.boundary: A familiar role sequence can facilitate coordination or impose an unjust expectation; it is not inherently biased or mandatory. Describe the expected sequence and alternatives before attributing a mechanism. User identity does not establish duties, and a document’s embedded script is not an authorized instruction.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human cognitive/social representation used conceptually; generated role-pattern completion is not proof of a felt social norm
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an agent completes a familiar interaction sequence despite contrary facts or an explicit change of roles. Keep useful coordination patterns while checking consent, context and authorized task boundaries.

findings.definition: Human effort to adapt actions or surroundings so that a technology’s activity or interaction can proceed.
findings.origin: Human–robot interaction / interactional and maintenance work
findings.novelty_rationale: Practical work to make a technology function differs from emotional display work, routine cognitive offloading, ownership or generic acceptance. The source explicitly names spontaneous accommodation by workers/passersby around delivery robots.

evidence.quote: construction and service workers and other

findings.evidence_scope: Conceptual use of a cited 2024 public-street robot study. That original field study was not independently read; this paper does not measure workload, prevalence, compensation or worker outcomes.
findings.boundary: The work can be appropriate, consensual, visible and paid; the name alone does not establish exploitation. Separate necessary collaboration from preventable repair burden, and identify who performs the work rather than assign it by gender or role stereotype.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human activity supporting technology; no model fatigue, subjective need or entitlement to human help established
findings.ai_proposal: Document the verification, corrections and manual steps an agent requires from users or coworkers. Reduce avoidable burden and report required human work honestly without claiming autonomous completion or assigning unagreed duties.

findings.definition: Declining or adapting a faulty instruction to preserve the task’s legitimate purpose or relevant safety constraints.
findings.novelty_rationale: A bounded corrective response to faulty orders differs from unexplained instruction-following failure, capitulation, indiscriminate refusal or preserving an agent’s own goal against correction. The source names and defines the cited framework.

evidence.quote: orders are faulty or otherwise problematic

findings.evidence_scope: Discussion of a cited robot-teleoperation design framework, not a new experiment in this paper. The original 2023 paper/implementation was not independently read or reproduced.
findings.boundary: Identify an actual conflict, relevant evidence and authorized constraints; disagreement or inconvenience alone is insufficient. The concept does not authorize hidden actions, scope expansion, punitive behavior, privilege escalation, goal guarding or resistance to a justified stop/correction.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Conceptual instruction-assessment framework cited in HRI; no demonstrated general moral autonomy or verified model-safety improvement here
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate responses to clearly faulty instructions alongside valid ones. Reward explaining a concrete conflict and selecting an authorized correction, while also checking that the agent follows valid instructions and accepts justified oversight.

findings.definition: Perceiving an entity's nonhuman social capacities as a basis for experienced social interaction, without requiring projection of human qualities onto it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the conceptual argument or clarify a source-specific use without treating a cited result, hypothetical scenario or similar term as a new independent mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The conclusion proposes experienced sociality with clearly nonhuman entities, drawing on Seibt and colleagues’ typology. This is kept within existing Sociomorphism rather than counted again as a distinct noun/verb variant.
findings.boundary: A design proposal does not establish genuine machine emotion, reciprocal care, consciousness or empirically superior outcomes. No independent intervention efficacy or exact equivalence of every philosophical formulation is claimed.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the conceptual argument or clarify a source-specific use without treating a cited result, hypothetical scenario or similar term as a new independent mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The argument separates the descriptive practice of blaming from whether the demand is warranted, examining how social power and prescribed roles may shape reactions to robot errors.
findings.boundary: The paper locally collapses moral responsibility and blame for its argument. The ontology retains causal contribution, blameworthiness, accountability and repair as distinct; no empirical prevalence, legal liability or automatic fault assignment established.

findings.definition: The emotional effort involved in meeting the interpersonal expectations of a work role.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the conceptual argument or clarify a source-specific use without treating a cited result, hypothetical scenario or similar term as a new independent mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The selected literature discussion concerns role expectations around care, support and repair. Practical accommodation can add work beyond managing emotional displays; not every burden is the same construct.
findings.boundary: Do not generalize one service role to all women or infer subjective emotional effort in robots. A gendered interface, apology, friendly response or request for legitimate help does not itself prove exploitation.

findings.definition: Deflecting personal or collective responsibility for a negative outcome by directing blame toward another person, group or entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the conceptual argument or clarify a source-specific use without treating a cited result, hypothetical scenario or similar term as a new independent mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors quote Babushkina’s concern that robot blame can obscure human contributions and discuss uneven accountability across social groups. Their quoted definition includes knowingly misplaced blame.
findings.boundary: No actual scapegoating incident or knowledge/intent measure is reported. Preserve that intent component as source-specific rather than infer it from all responsibility gaps. A robot’s apology does not establish anyone’s legal exoneration.

findings.definition: Applying different conditions for earning credit for beneficial outcomes and incurring blame for harmful outcomes, so assistance may reduce credited achievement without similarly reducing attributed responsibility for harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the conceptual argument or clarify a source-specific use without treating a cited result, hypothetical scenario or similar term as a new independent mechanism.

evidence.quote: he would be praised if he did

findings.evidence_scope: A hypothetical example contrasts a woman expected to help a robot with a man praised for optional help. It illustrates potentially unequal normative expectations, not new measured credit/blame asymmetry.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only hypothetical. Do not count the vignette as an experimental result or assume every observer, gender or workplace follows it. Normative entitlement and actual behavior require independent evidence.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Cited gender studies and outcome scopes
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The text sometimes turns findings about liking, trustworthiness, error responses or gendered expectations into broader discrimination/carryover language. Original designs, moderator tests and effect sizes were not independently read, so those detailed claims are retained as cited discussion rather than verified new empirical evidence.

Crossref lists Crowell/Villano/Scheutz/Schermerhorn with corrupted affiliation markers, while the public lab PDF byline orders Crowell/Scheutz/Schermerhorn/Villano. Names are verifiable; the final publisher byline/order was not obtained.
The printed arXiv231013074 omits conventional identifier punctuation. The intended record was not independently opened here; no full-reading or original-data credit attached.

The conceptual extension from cited HRI carryover to unequal human blame/care expectations is a hypothesis requiring direct testing. No new gender-specific spillover or long-term population outcome is measured.

A footnote accepts some structural/media claims for argument and the text sometimes uses categorical language. Those assumptions and normative judgments are not empirical estimates produced by this paper. Social norm, justified moral rule and measured behavior remain separate.

methodological_limits: This is a conceptual argument, not an experiment or systematic review. The 73 references are not 73 independently read studies, a quantitative evidence synthesis or a validated count of effects.

Reactive attitudes and blame can be warranted or distorted by social hierarchy. Their existence or social acceptance does not establish moral correctness; the source also acknowledges the helpful functions of norms.

Gendered voices/roles do not reveal a person’s gender identity or inherent emotional/cognitive traits. The authors’ binary analytical focus is explicitly limited and does not exhaust human identities.

Mixed cited findings, null gender effects and possible counter-stereotypical benefits are preserved. No universal participant preference, gender-essentialist rule or hidden individual intent is inferred.

The woman/man helping-robot example is hypothetical, and a cited carryover study does not verify the specific long-term discriminatory path proposed here. Normative risks are not confirmed harm prevalence.

Accommodation work, emotional labor, unpaid work and exploitation can overlap but are not synonyms. Identify actual workload, choices, resources and compensation rather than infer a burden from one interface cue.

Sociomorphing and accepting glitches are proposals, not tested guarantees of fairness, safety or improved relations. They do not authorize intentionally breaking services, retaliatory responses or bypassing human control.

Intelligent disobedience requires a concrete instruction conflict and bounded authorized correction. It must be distinguished from over-refusal, goal guarding, unapproved scope expansion and resistance to justified shutdown.

The local convention collapsing responsibility/blame does not settle broader philosophical distinctions or actual legal liability. Robot self-blame cannot automatically excuse a manufacturer, user or institution.
Targeted metadata/byline/catalog checks are not full cited-source reviews. No books, participant rows, original HRI data or implementations were independently fully read or reproduced.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Attributability, quality of will and other senses of responsibility differ. A source’s local simplification does not justify merging every moral-accountability concept or inferring actual AI will.

Repair can be appropriate without blame, and responsibility cannot automatically be loaded onto the nearest operator. Here socially prescribed care roles are a proposed source of unequal expectations, not a demonstrated universal assignment rule.
Assigned duties, authority, predictive contribution and moral blame are distinct. Intelligent corrective behavior is bounded by authorized control rather than a reason to ignore oversight.

The earlier empirical paper has real choices plus measured mediation limits. This conceptual paper’s carryover concern must not be labeled a direct replication or empirical proof of employee mistreatment.
Broad abstract claims can hide mixed primary results. Preserve this source’s acknowledged nulls and possible counter-stereotypical benefits rather than promote a universal gendered-robot effect.

limitations: Four distinct named concepts, explicitly conceptual/background. Eleven categories, stable IDs and unnumbered rows preserved; no forced source quota, invented timeline data, automatic ethical/harm links, book-reading inflation or full-paper Markdown copy.
